# Arhat in 2026: why scholars still care

Names are not only data points; they are cultural ​evidence. **Arhat** shows why an ASCII spelling can still demand serious scholarship. The sources distinguish this name from every neighboring form, and the temple records that distinction without adding marks the evidence ‌does not contain. What follows is the full picture — name, script, sound, myth, cult, and legacy — ending with the digital home that makes the record easy to reach.

## Overview

​**Arhat** (*arhat*) — Worthy One, Saint · an Arhat or superior divinity with the Jainas — belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Worthy One, Saint". The ​name means "an Arhat or superior divinity with the Jainas".

The **arhat** is the ideal of early Buddhism made flesh: one who has **destroyed the taints, done what had to be done, ​and laid down the burden** — freedom achieved in this life, by this person, without a god's intervention. The Theragāthā lets the finished saints speak for themselves.

## Mythology

The stories of Arhat place worthy one, saint at the center of a living mythological world.

### ​Origins (Myth)

Arhat appears in buddhist tradition as worthy one, saint. The name's meaning, "an Arhat or superior divinity with the Jainas", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory ​(Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Arhat in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Arhat survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. ​Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare ​them. The restoration Arhat gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Worthy of Gifts (The Word)

**Arhat** comes from √*arh*, "to deserve, to be worthy," with the participle ‌-at — "the worthy one," one deserving of the alms of gods and men. The Buddha claimed it as his own foremost title: in the canonical litany he is *arahaṃ sammāsambuddho*, "arahant, fully ​self-awakened" — a claim whose audacity the *Udāna* records being tested in his lifetime, when rivals demanded he prove it. The commentarial definition sharpens the word into a checklist: one who has ‌destroyed the taints (*āsava*), lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, and knows "there is no more of this." The Jaina tradition uses the same ​word in parallel: its twenty-four *tīrthaṅkaras* are *arhats*, worthy ones who ford the flood of rebirth. The mythic weight of a title: Buddhism made holiness a **completed task, not a birth** — ‌and gave it a word anyone could check.

### Sāriputta and Moggallāna (The Chiefs)

The Buddha named his two greatest arahants in the *Etadagga* verses (AN 1): **Sāriputta**, foremost in great wisdom — ​the Dhamma's marshal, who could unfold a single line into a hundred meanings and who, questioned on his deathbed in the *Sāriputta Sutta* (SN 47.19), replied only that there was nowhere he ‌had ever clung; and **Moggallāna**, foremost in psychic powers, who humbled Brahmā's pride by shaking the Vejayanta palace with a toe (DN 11, *Kevaṭṭa Sutta*). Both were murdered — Moggallāna beaten to ​death by brigands — the Buddha predicting that the pair would die as the twin sāla trees fall. The *Theragāthā* lets the arahants speak in their own voices: "Cut down the whole forest ‌of craving, not just one tree; from the jungle of craving, fear is born." The ideal is given a human face twice — the thinker and the wonder-worker — and both faces ​end in the one death arahants cannot refuse.

### Four Gates to the Deathless (The Path)

Arahantship is the fourth and last gate. The canon maps the road precisely: the **stream-enterer** (sotāpanna), certain ​of awakening, never again reborn lower than human; the **once-returner** (sakadāgāmin), who comes back once to this world; the **non-returner** (anāgāmin), who awakens in a higher heaven and does not return at ‌all; and the **arahant**, freed here and now. The decisive faculty is stated everywhere and nowhere better than the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta* (MN 10): mindfulness of body, feelings, mind, and dhammas — "the ‌direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow." Fifteen centuries later Buddhaghosa's *Visuddhimagga* (5th c. CE) welded the whole road into one manual, still the map of Theravāda ‌practice. The interpretive core: holiness is **gradual, inspectable, and irreversible** — a ladder whose rungs can be named, and whose top rung is the end of needing anything, forever.

## Symbols & Iconography

​The iconography associated with Arhat concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Arhat, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** ​— Worthy One, Saint

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Arhat across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a ‌claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Arhat carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The begging bowl** — The arhat's only possession — and the reason the laity feed ​him: the worthy one is a field of merit, and a donation ripens
- **The crutch and long eyebrows** — The lohans' immortal attributes in Chinese art — longevity so extreme it needs ​support, and sight so deep it overgrows
- **The flame of the taints extinguished** — Nirvāṇa as a fire gone out — the arhat is the one whose fuel (rāga, dosa, moha) is ‌spent; nothing more burns
- **The lion's roar of assurance** — The arhat's declaration 'there is no more coming to any state of being' — certainty spoken from completion, not faith
- **The assembly ​of elders** — Sāriputta and Moggallāna flanking the Buddha — wisdom and powers as the twin pillars of the arhat ideal

## A Meditation

The arhat is the most austere ‌ideal any major religion has proposed: not love, not justice, not obedience — **completion**. The canonical formula is brutal in its economy: done is what had to be done; there is no ‌more of this. No god approves it, no history rewards it, no heaven awaits as payment. It is simply over.

That is why the Mahāyāna found it both admirable and insufficient, and ‌why modern readers find it quietly devastating. The arhat does not save the world; the arhat leaves. Yet the tradition kept the begging bowl — the one object that binds the finished saint ‌back to the unfinished crowd, who must feed him and so plant their own merit. Perfection, the bowl insists, is not private. The worthy one stands at the door precisely so that ​someone else can practice giving. The ideal of having nothing, it turns out, was always also a technology of **connection**.
